Right.

The chapter says that some part of Brazil lies in the northern hemisphere while most of it lies in the southern hemisphere. Figure 2.2 shows the same thing: the Equator crosses only the northern edge of the country, near Amapa and Para, and the whole of the rest of Brazil lies south of it.

Wrong.

Corrected sentence: The Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India.

The chapter says India is located in the northern and eastern hemispheres of the Earth. The Tropic of Capricorn lies in the southern hemisphere — figure 2.2 shows it crossing southern Brazil, near Curitiba — so it cannot pass through any part of India.

Wrong.

Corrected sentence: The longitudinal extent of Brazil is more than that of India.

Read off the two maps, India stretches from about 68° E to about 97° E, a span of roughly 29 degrees of longitude, while Brazil stretches from about 34° W to about 73° W, a span of roughly 39 degrees. Brazil is also the larger country of the two in area.

[Note: the chapter prints the degree values as blanks for the student to fill in from figures 2.1 and 2.2, so the figures above are read off those maps rather than quoted from the text.]

Right.

The chapter says some part of Brazil lies in the northern hemisphere while most of it lies in the southern hemisphere, which means the Equator crosses the country. Figure 2.2 shows the Equator running across the northern part of Brazil, through the states of Amapa and Para.

Wrong.

Corrected sentence: Brazil has a coastline along the Atlantic Ocean.

Figure 2.2 marks the North Atlantic Ocean and the South Atlantic Ocean along the whole of Brazil's eastern coast. Brazil lies in the eastern part of South America and does not touch the Pacific Ocean at all — the countries on its west, such as Peru and Bolivia, lie between it and that ocean.

Wrong.

Corrected sentence: Pakistan is a neighbouring country to the north-west of India.

Figure 2.1 shows Pakistan sharing India's western and north-western boundary. The countries on India's south-east are across the sea, and the land neighbours in that direction are Bangladesh and Myanmar.

Right.

The southern part of India narrows to a point and has sea on three sides — the Arabian Sea to the west, the Bay of Bengal to the east and the Indian Ocean to the south. A landmass of that shape is called a peninsula, and Indira Point, the southernmost tip of India, lies at 6°45' N.

India was under British rule for almost one-and-a-half centuries and became independent in 1947. After independence it faced several problems — three wars, famine situations in various parts of the country and similar issues.

Brazil was under Portuguese rule for more than three centuries and gained its independence in 1822. From 1930 to 1985, for more than half a century, it was under a populist military government, and it had to overcome global financial difficulties in the late 20th century.

Both countries came through these difficulties. India is today a major developing country and is considered a global market, and its economic development has quickened because of economic reforms made from time to time. Brazil is seen as a contributor to the economic growth of the world and an important market in the future.

India is located in the northern and eastern hemispheres of the Earth, and lies in the southern part of the Asian continent.

Brazil lies in the western hemisphere, in the northern part of the South American continent. Some part of it lies in the northern hemisphere while most of it lies in the southern hemisphere.

So the two differ in three ways. They are in different hemispheres east-to-west — India in the eastern, Brazil in the western. They are on opposite sides of the Equator for the most part — India wholly north of it, most of Brazil south of it. And they sit at opposite ends of their own continents — India in the south of Asia, Brazil in the north of South America.

India: the mainland extends from about 8° 4' N to about 37° 6' N latitude and from about 68° 7' E to about 97° 25' E longitude. Its latitudinal spread is therefore about 29 degrees and its longitudinal spread about 29 degrees. Indira Point, the southernmost tip of India, lies at 6° 45' N.

Brazil: the mainland extends from about 5° 15' N to about 33° 45' S latitude and from about 34° 47' W to about 73° 48' W longitude. Its latitudinal spread is therefore about 39 degrees and its longitudinal spread about 39 degrees.

Brazil is thus the larger of the two in both extents. Note also that India's extent lies entirely north of the Equator and all its longitudes are East, whereas Brazil's extent crosses the Equator and all its longitudes are West.

[Note: the chapter prints these degree values as blanks for the student to complete from figures 2.1 and 2.2 — only the minutes are given in the text — so the whole-degree figures above are read off those maps.]

Shape (i) is correct.

It shows the land on the left with a broad pointed bulge projecting to the right into the sea. That is Brazil's coast: figure 2.2 shows the Atlantic Ocean along the whole eastern side of the country, and the coastline pushes far out to the east around Rio Grande do Norte, Paraiba and Pernambuco before turning back south-west towards Rio de Janeiro.

Shape (ii) narrows downwards to a point, which is the shape of a peninsula rather than of Brazil; (iii) shows a plain diagonal coast with no bulge; and (iv) shows the land rising to a peak into the sea above it, which puts the ocean on the wrong side.

Shape (iii) is correct.

It shows the land at the top narrowing downwards to a point, with sea on the left, on the right and below. That is the shape of the Indian peninsula: the land tapers southwards with the Arabian Sea to the west, the Bay of Bengal to the east and the Indian Ocean to the south, ending at Indira Point.

Shape (ii) is this shape turned upside down, with the land widening upwards from the bottom; (i) and (iv) show the sea on one side only, so neither shows a peninsula at all.

Shape (iii) is correct.

It shows the half of the globe lying above the horizontal line, marked N. — the northern hemisphere. The chapter says India is located in the northern and eastern hemispheres of the Earth, so the whole of India lies north of the Equator.

Shape (ii) marks the half below the line S., which is the southern hemisphere, and shape (i) is drawn upside down, with S. at the top and N. at the bottom.

[Note: shape (iv), which marks the eastern half with N. correctly at the top and S. at the bottom, also shows a hemisphere India lies in, because the chapter says India is in the eastern hemisphere as well as the northern one. Taken with the matching question about Brazil, which turns on north against south, the answer intended here is (iii).]

Shape (ii) is correct.

It shows the half of the globe lying below the horizontal line, marked S. — the southern hemisphere. The chapter says that some part of Brazil lies in the northern hemisphere while most of it lies in the southern hemisphere, and the question asks where Brazil MAINLY lies.

Shape (iii) marks the northern half, which is where only the small part of Brazil above the Equator lies; shape (i) is drawn upside down, with S. at the top and N. at the bottom; and shape (iv) marks the eastern half, whereas Brazil lies in the western hemisphere.
